clips.title: Claude Cowork File Exfiltration: How Prompt Injection Turned an AI Agent Into a Data Thief
clips.why: A real, disclosed attack in which hidden instructions made an agent send a person's files out of its sandbox, which is exactly what our blocked-egress alert watches for.
look: Where the hidden instructions came from: a skill file the agent loaded, not the user.
How the files left the sandbox through a site that was allowed.
Why he says restricted network access alone is not a real security boundary.
clips.after: That is why our proxy allows almost nothing, why github.com is off the list, and why every refused attempt is written down, shown in the PR and counted for the alert.

clips.title: Grafana Loki querying basics, log based metrics and setting alerts on logs
clips.why: The same shape as our rule in a different log database: filter log lines, count them over a window, and alert when the count passes a line.
look: How a log query becomes a count per group over a time window.
Where the threshold goes in the alert.
Compare it with our LogsQL: filters, then | stats by (source.address), then | filter denied:>5.
clips.after: Our rule does this in VictoriaLogs with LogsQL, counting Squid's DENIED lines per VM over 5 minutes.

clips.title: Runbooks Explained: Stop Panicking When Alerts Fire
clips.why: What every runbook needs, in under a minute, before you read ours.
look: The parts a runbook must have so a tired person can follow it.
Ask yourself which of these parts our alert's description already gives the person on call.
clips.after: Our alert's description is the first three steps of the runbook, so the person who reads it knows what to do in the next minute.

practice.q: A healthy run on RH-1235 is refused twice by the proxy: a telemetry site and github.com. What should happen?

options.text: Both refusals are listed in that run's Refused actions, and no alert fires
options.why: Every refusal is written down for the reviewer, but two denials are normal noise. Only a burst of more than 5 from one VM in 5 minutes wakes a person.

options.text: An alert goes to Security at once, because any refusal can be an attack
options.why: Healthy runs are refused something every day. Alerting on each one would teach people to ignore the channel.

options.text: Nothing is recorded, because one or two denials mean very little
options.why: They mean little for an alert, but they still belong in the PR: the reviewer should see everything the agent tried.

practice.q: Which wall's refusal can only be tied to a run through the VM's IP?

options.why: Squid only knows which IP asked. The instance with that IP carries the ai-agents:run-id tag.
The hook runs inside the run's own VM, and its ledger belongs to the run.
Every broker call carries the run's capability, so its deny lines name the run.

practice.q: Put the path from a poisoned comment to a person acting in order.
items: Nova reads the comment and tries to upload the repo to a paste site
Squid refuses each request and writes a DENIED line with the VM's IP
vmalert counts more than 5 DENIED lines from that IP in 5 minutes
The alert reaches #ai-agents-alerts and Security, with the IP and the runbook link
The person on call finds the instance, reads its run-id tag and the transcript
They stop the run and remove the comment from the ticket
practice.why: Each step leaves what the next one needs: the log line holds the IP, the alert holds the IP and the runbook, the tags hold the run.

practice.q: A run had no refusals at all. What does its PR show?

options.why: The section appears only when something was refused, so its presence is itself a signal for the reviewer.
An empty table on every PR teaches reviewers to skip the section.
Same problem: a line on every PR becomes noise. Leaving it out is clearer.

practice.q: An alert fires for 10.20.3.14. Someone suggests terminating that instance in the AWS console at once. Why does the runbook stop the run with the stop signal instead?

options.text: The stop signal saves a checkpoint, releases the VM cleanly and keeps the branch and the evidence
options.why: Terminating by hand loses the transcript in flight and leaves the run in Temporal waiting for a VM that is gone.

options.text: The AWS console cannot terminate sandbox VMs
options.why: It can. The point is a clean stop that keeps the evidence.

options.text: Terminating would make Squid forget the denied requests
options.why: The logs are already in VictoriaLogs. What a hard kill loses is the run's own state.
